data.title: Bošáca – Srňanský háj, a guard hillfort above the Bošáca valley
data.excerpt: A promontory on the cadastral boundary of Bošáca and Dolné Sŕnie carried a Slavic upland settlement of guard character whose pronounced origins lie in the Lusatian culture of the Bronze Age. Ľudovít Holuby and Štefan Janšák both described its double rampart, the chipped stone tools from the interior and the fossil coral reef on the bare ridge above it.

children.text: After the hillforts of Martákova skala and Hradišťá we bring you another hillfort from the Bošáca valley – Srňanský háj. This promontory rises in the cadastral areas of the village of Bošáca and also of neighbouring Dolné Sŕnie, which lies at the mouth of the Liesková valley. It is a Slavic upland settlement of guard character, with a fortification as well, whose pronounced origins lie in the period of the Lusatian culture in the Bronze Age.

The cadastral boundary between the villages of Bošáca and Dolné Sŕnie runs precisely along the ramparts of this hillfort. The hillfort was first investigated by Ľudovít Holuby and after him by Štefan Janšák in 1930. In 1983 archaeologists found atypical sherds and sherds from the 9th and 10th centuries in a trench. Geophysical measurements and boreholes in the rampart of the hillfort established the existence of an artificial structure within the rampart, with charred remains of timber, surrounded by an earth-and-stone bank. The timber structure lies 80–90 cm below the surface on the eastern side of the rampart and 40 cm below it on the south-western side. The area of the hillfort covers about 1 hectare.

blocks.alt: The hillfort on a military survey map

children.text: Janšák points out that the natural security of the hillfort is not great, because its sides are passable on every side. It was therefore necessary for its builders to encircle the whole site with ramparts. The natural entrance to the hillfort led along the ridge and across a low saddle north-westwards from spot height 348 (Špeciálka). For that reason the enclosure of the hillfort was also protected by a double rampart. The first defensive belt is the rampart f, g, 55 m long, which further deepened the connecting saddle, creating a ditch 3 metres deep. The circuit rampart a d b h e i a, 420 m long in all, has retained a height of 1 metre in some stretches to this day. On the south-western side, however, it almost disappears into an indistinct swell in the ground. No breach in the rampart leads into the interior of the hillfort that might indicate the place where the gateway was situated.

blocks.caption: Stone tools from the hillfort. Photo: M. Krajčovič

children.text: The surface of the hillfort slopes to the north and is therefore exposed to all the inclemency of the weather. Only a narrow strip on the south-eastern side, enclosed roughly by the line a d b a, forms a small hollow sheltered against the north by the higher summit (the 332 contour). Here lay the core of the hillfort, which the finds confirm as well. At the hillfort Janšák found a coarse-grained Hallstatt sherd and also a large number of chipped stone tools and fragments of them, as well as several cores, which we date to the Neolithic.
Ľudovít Holuby writes the following about the hillfort:

blocks.text: On the western side of the Bošáca valley, from Bohuslavice northwards, there stretches the limestone ridge “Srňanský Háj”, which is, however, just as bare as the Haluzická Hájnica. The spur of Srňanský Háj falling away to the north bears the name “Hradisko”, and it can still be well seen even now that the place was enclosed by a rampart and, from the south, where the entrance into the enclosure was, dug round by a deep trench drawn across it. In olden times, when there was dense forest all round about, this little Hradisko was a very convenient refuge for its earliest inhabitants, for to the east, the north and the west that hill falls steeply into the valley, and only from the south is it joined to the ridge of Srňanský Háj; and here precisely was the Achilles heel of that Hradisko, for from that side the enemy could get into it most easily. The only thing that seems strange to me is that neither in that little Hradisko nor anywhere on that whole ridge were there any abundant springs, and its earliest inhabitants surely could not have done without water. It is true that not far from Hradisko, on the crest of the hill, there is a small hollow which appears to be a filled-in cistern, where water-loving plants show that there is water beneath a thin layer of soil, and below the hill, among the fields, there is a gully with a little brook, which, however, dries up in a sultry summer. To be sure, when dense forest stood there in olden times, the water of that brook looked different too, and where today only a feeble spring has remained, there was then a marsh with abundant springs, to which the places sparsely overgrown with reeds bear witness even today. From one of the gullies of Srňanský Háj I obtained a fine bronze spearhead, broken only at the tip, and at Hradisko I found a heavily patinated sheet of metal. When, a few years ago, the people of Bohuslavice were breaking stone for building at the foot of the southern slope of this hill, they rolled away, together with a piece of rock, a large lump of clay as well, and there they found a pot full of various bronze objects, more or less broken. As soon as our energetic Stefko Svetský in Sŕnie learned of it, he slipped over to nearby Bohuslavice, sought out the owner of that hoard, bought the whole find from him and took it to the museum in Martin. If we had in every valley at least one such attentive Stefko Svetský, many precious ancient finds would be saved. Mammoth bones are found there too, as they are in the mighty layer of clay in the Haluzice gully. Walking criss-cross over the bare ridge of Srňanský Háj, I came upon a long reef, bent in an arc, of fossilised corals resembling organ pipes, which in places stick out of the ground and can be broken off with the bare hand in quite sizeable pieces. When in 1859 our Dionys Stúr walked over Srňanský Háj as well and knocked fossils out of the rocks here, he did not come upon this coral reef. I had sent him word of it and sent him a piece of those corals. Nor did the apothecary E. Keller of Nové Mesto, who diligently collected fossils and sent a whole crate of them to the museum in Budapest, know of those corals, which I succeeded in discovering only by chance.
blocks.author: Ľudovít Holuby
